## Schema — `10k_seanchai_register_schema.sql`

### Tables

```sql
-- People
CREATE TABLE seanchai.people (
    id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    slug        TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,         -- e.g. 'phelim-oboyle'
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    alt_name    TEXT,
    person_group TEXT NOT NULL,               -- sidebar section heading
    born_year   TEXT,                         -- 'c. 1748', '1773 or 1777'
    born_place  TEXT,
    died_year   TEXT,
    died_place  TEXT,
    notes       TEXT
);

-- Places
CREATE TABLE seanchai.places (
    id               SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    slug             TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,    -- e.g. 'romania-farm'
    name             TEXT NOT NULL,
    alt_name         TEXT,
    place_group      TEXT NOT NULL,           -- sidebar section heading
    place_type       TEXT,                    -- 'farm', 'township', 'city', etc.
    loc_area         TEXT,
    loc_county       TEXT,
    loc_state        TEXT,
    loc_country      TEXT,
    established_year TEXT,
    established_note TEXT,
    status_year      TEXT,
    status_note      TEXT,
    current_status   TEXT,
    notes            TEXT
);

-- Events (one row per event per person)
CREATE TABLE seanchai.person_events (
    id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    person_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seanchai.people(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    event_year  TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_text  TEXT NOT NULL,
    sort_order  INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

-- Events (one row per event per place)
CREATE TABLE seanchai.place_events (
    id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    place_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seanchai.places(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    event_year  TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_text  TEXT NOT NULL,
    sort_order  INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

-- Person↔Person relationships
-- All four directions stored as stated in the artifact (parent/child/spouse/sibling)
CREATE TABLE seanchai.person_relationships (
    person_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seanchai.people(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    related_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seanchai.people(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    kind        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('parent','child','spouse','sibling')),
    PRIMARY KEY (person_id, related_id, kind)
);

-- Person↔Place associations (associatedPlaces / associatedPeople)
CREATE TABLE seanchai.person_place_assoc (
    person_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seanchai.people(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    place_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seanchai.places(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    PRIMARY KEY (person_id, place_id)
);

-- Place↔Place relations
CREATE TABLE seanchai.place_relations (
    place_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seanchai.places(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    related_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seanchai.places(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    PRIMARY KEY (place_id, related_id)
);

-- Tags (junction tables — consistent with rest of schema)
CREATE TABLE seanchai.person_tags (
    person_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seanchai.people(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    tag         TEXT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (person_id, tag)
);

CREATE TABLE seanchai.place_tags (
    place_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seanchai.places(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    tag         TEXT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (place_id, tag)
);
```

### GRANTs (end of `10k`)

```sql
GRANT SELECT ON
    seanchai.people,
    seanchai.places,
    seanchai.person_events,
    seanchai.place_events,
    seanchai.person_relationships,
    seanchai.person_place_assoc,
    seanchai.place_relations,
    seanchai.person_tags,
    seanchai.place_tags
TO web_app_user;
```

---

## Data — what to extract from the artifact

Read `https://claude.ai/artifact/U6ubhT3cx4TXqg58bik4dR` with the Artifact tool.  
The artifact contains hardcoded `PEOPLE` (25 records) and `PLACES` (21 records) JS arrays.

### People (25 records in 5 groups)

| Group | Slugs |
|---|---|
| Boyle — Donegal Line | `phelim-oboyle`, `ann-rice`, `felix-sr-boyle`, `connell-boyle`, `john-boyle-1804`, `maria-boyle` |
| Beall Line | `major-zephaniah-beall`, `zephaniah-beall-esq`, `mary-purcell`, `rebecca-beall` |
| Connell's Children | `captain-felix`, `zephaniah-m-boyle`, `john-d-boyle-sr`, `john-boyle-jr`, `constantine-boyle`, `mary-boyle-1846`, `annie-boyle` |
| Captain Felix's Family | `mary-ann-oneill`, `paul-mary-boyle`, `nellie-carlin`, `felix-michael`, `robert-emmett-boyle` |
| Felix Michael's Family | `ida-ohara`, `charles-emmett-uncle`, `robert-lawrence` |

**Person fields:** id (text slug), name, altName, group, tags[], associatedPlaces[], born{year (TEXT), place}, died{year (TEXT), place}, parents[], spouse[], children[], siblings[], events[{year (TEXT), text}], notes

### Places (21 records in 5 groups)

| Group | Slugs |
|---|---|
| Monongahela River Sites | `romania-farm`, `lock-no-4` |
| Washington County | `carroll-township`, `boyle-family-cemetery`, `east-pike-run-distillery`, `fallowfield-township`, `beallsville`, `canonsburg`, `washington-pa`, `brownsville-fayette` |
| Pittsburgh & Allegheny County | `elizabethtown-pa`, `homestead`, `point-state-park`, `munhall`, `carnegie-tech`, `brehm-road` |
| Ireland | `killygordon-donegal` |
| Beyond Pennsylvania | `red-river-louisiana`, `national-military-home-dayton`, `thunder-bay-ontario`, `fort-belvoir-va` |

**Place fields:** id (text slug), name, altName, group, type, tags[], location{area, county, state, country}, established{year (TEXT), note}, status{year (TEXT), note}, currentStatus, associatedPeople[], relatedPlaces[], events[{year (TEXT), text}], notes

**Years are TEXT throughout — never coerce to integers.**

---

## Seed SQL strategy for `10l`

Build the seed in this order:

1. INSERT all 25 `seanchai.people` rows (slug, name, alt_name, person_group, born_year, born_place, died_year, died_place, notes) — use slug as the stable key
2. INSERT all 21 `seanchai.places` rows (slug, name, alt_name, place_group, place_type, loc_*, established_*, status_*, current_status, notes)
3. INSERT `seanchai.person_events` — join to people by slug via subselect
4. INSERT `seanchai.place_events` — join to places by slug via subselect
5. INSERT `seanchai.person_relationships` — join both slugs via subselect
6. INSERT `seanchai.person_place_assoc` — join both slugs via subselect
7. INSERT `seanchai.place_relations` — join both slugs via subselect
8. INSERT `seanchai.person_tags`
9. INSERT `seanchai.place_tags`

**Subselect pattern for slug resolution (use consistently):**

```sql
INSERT INTO seanchai.person_events (person_id, event_year, event_text, sort_order)
SELECT p.id, 'c. 1748', 'Born in County Donegal, Ireland', 1
FROM seanchai.people p WHERE p.slug = 'phelim-oboyle';
```

## 📄 DESIGN_MESSAGES_SCHEMA_SPARKS

# Design Doc — Messages Schema ("The Sparks")

**Status:** Design only. Assumes the multi-role identity refactor
(see `DESIGN_MULTI_ROLE_IDENTITY.md`) is already in place — Sparks is
built as an *additive* crew role from day one, not bolted onto the old
single-role model.

**Naming:** Schema and tables use plain functional nouns (`messages`),
consistent with `identity`/`projects`/`audit`. "The Sparks" is the
crew-role display name and landing-card label only — same layer as
Captain/Mechanic/Envoy/Scribe, not the schema name. This keeps the
`/crew/{entity}/...` route convention and schema-naming convention
both intact; theming stays confined to the display layer as already
decided for the future crew-terminology work.

---

## Schema

### `messages.notification_level` (lookup table)

```
id         BIGINT PK
name       VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE   -- e.g. 'silent', 'normal', 'urgent'
rings_bell BOOLEAN              -- whether this level fires pg_notify at all
```

Values span from "do nothing" (recorded in the message center, no
outbound ping) up through "ring all the alarm bells" (immediate
Apprise dispatch). `rings_bell` is the flag `api.create_message()`
checks to decide whether to call `pg_notify` at all — every message
gets a row regardless of level; only some levels also trigger a push.

Open question carried over from the failure-modes discussion: should
certain sources (e.g. anything tagged `source = 'audit'`) have a
floor — a minimum notification level that can't be configured below —
so a security event can never be silently downgraded to "do nothing"
by a lookup-table edit? If so, that constraint lives in
`api.create_message()`'s logic, not in the lookup table itself, which
just holds the available levels.

### `messages.messages`

```
id               BIGINT PK
recipient_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES identity.app_user (id)
sender_label     TEXT              -- not an FK; external senders
                                    -- ("audit trigger", "customer
                                    -- question form") aren't app_users
subject          TEXT NOT NULL
body             TEXT
source           VARCHAR(50)       -- 'audit', 'customer_question',
                                    -- 'inbound_email', etc.
notification_level_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES messages.notification_level (id)
read_at          TIMESTAMPTZ       -- NULL = unread
created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
```

`recipient_id` is always the actual authenticated `app_user` — never
a client-supplied value trusted at read time (see `api.*` functions
below).

### `messages.v_message_detail`

Whitelisted view for the detail panel, following the existing
`v_*_detail` convention — `id` and `*_by`-style columns excluded,
column order matches intended field order. Realistically the only
"editable" field here is `read_at` (marking read), so this view is
mostly for display, not a general-purpose edit form.

---

## `api.*` functions

- **`api.create_message(payload JSONB)`** — the single write path
  every producer (audit trigger, customer-question handler, future
  inbound-email Worker) calls. Inserts the row; if the resolved
  `notification_level.rings_bell` is true, calls `pg_notify('new_message',
  ...)` with enough payload for the listener to act without a second
  query. This is where "was created" and "should notify" are decided
  together, at the database layer — no producer needs to know Apprise
  exists.
- **`api.get_messages_for_user(p_user_id BIGINT)`** — returns every
  message where `recipient_id = p_user_id`. `p_user_id` comes from the
  authenticated session, never trusted as a raw client parameter, same
  defensive posture as the rest of `api.*`.
- **`api.mark_message_read(p_message_id BIGINT, p_user_id BIGINT)`** —
  sets `read_at`, but only after confirming the message actually
  belongs to `p_user_id`. Returns `NULL`/an error shape if it doesn't,
  rather than silently succeeding on someone else's message.

All three follow the existing `06d_api_grants.sql` pattern —
`web_app_user` gets `EXECUTE`, nothing else; no direct table/view
grants, consistent with the rest of `api.*`.

---

## Landing card / role tie-in

- Sparks becomes a row in `identity.crew_role`, assignable via the
  (now multi-valued) `identity.app_user_crew_role` join table, same as
  any other role.
- A user holding Sparks gets a "Sparks" card on their landing page
  (via the existing `identity.landing_card`-style mechanism, or
  whatever the landing-card design lands on), routing to a new
  `/crew/messages/...` or similar path — the panel shows
  `api.get_messages_for_user()` results, most-recent first, unread
  visually distinct.
- Mesh + login gating is inherited for free from Curator's existing
  auth — no new access-control code needed here specifically, per the
  "reuse, don't rebuild" conclusion reached earlier.

---

## Open questions

1. **Does marking a message read need to be undoable** (mark unread
   again), or is `read_at` a one-way flag?
2. **Retention** — do old, read messages ever get purged/archived, or
   does this table grow forever? Not urgent at low volume, but worth a
   stated answer rather than an implicit "we'll deal with it later."
3. **Does every crew member with Sparks see *all* messages addressed
   to them regardless of source**, or does Sparks itself need
   sub-filtering (e.g. Felipe only sees `customer_question` and
   `inbound_email` messages, not internal audit alerts meant for you)?
   This may push `recipient_id` scoping to need a `source` allowlist
   per user, which isn't in the schema above yet.
4. **Notification-level floor enforcement** (carried over from
   above) — decide before `create_message()` is written, since it
   changes the function's logic, not just its schema.

## 📄 DESIGN_MESSAGE_CENTER_NOTIFICATION_HUB

# Design Doc — Message Center ↔ Notification Hub Interaction

**Status:** Design only. Covers how the Messages schema (persistent,
mesh-gated, queryable) and Apprise (stateless, one-directional
dispatcher) fit together, plus the failure modes this design needs to
account for.

---

## Core distinction

Apprise is not a message store and has no memory of past calls — it
receives "send this notification" and dispatches outward (Telegram,
email, SMS). It never gets queried later for history. The **message
center** (the `messages` schema from `DESIGN_MESSAGES_SCHEMA_SPARKS.md`)
is the durable, retrievable record; Apprise is the side-effect that
pings a phone.

Not every event needs both halves. Producers split into two
categories:

**Category 1 — persisted + notified.** Customer questions, audit-trail
alerts, inbound email — anything someone should be able to log into
Curator later and review. These write through `api.create_message()`,
which conditionally fires `pg_notify` based on the message's
notification level.

**Category 2 — fire-and-forget, no persistence.** Ephemeral
infrastructure pings (disk usage, a failed systemd unit) with no
lasting value in a "read again later" sense. These call Apprise
directly — no `messages` schema involvement.

```
Category 1 producers                Category 2 producers
(audit trigger, customer form,       (disk check, systemd watcher,
 inbound-email Worker)                anything ephemeral)
        │                                    │
        ▼                                    │
  api.create_message()                       │
   (INSERT + conditional pg_notify)          │
        │                                    │
        ▼                                    │
  Python LISTEN process                      │
        │                                    │
        └──────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                        ▼
                 Apprise REST API
                  (tag-based routing)
                        │
                        ▼
           Telegram / Email / SMS, per tag config
```

---

## Failure modes and mitigations

### 1. Silent notification loss at the LISTEN boundary
`pg_notify` is fire-and-forget, not a queue — if the listener isn't
connected at the exact moment `NOTIFY` fires (restart, blip, Postgres
bounce), that signal is gone permanently. The message row is safe
(durable INSERT); the "tell someone" signal is not.

*Mitigation:* `Restart=always` on the listener's systemd unit shrinks
the vulnerable window but doesn't close it. Closing it needs a second,
independent mechanism — a systemd *timer* unit running a periodic
sweep of `messages.messages` for rows above the notification floor
with no recorded "notification sent" confirmation, re-firing those.
This requires `create_message()`/the listener to actually record
successful dispatch somewhere (a `notified_at` column, or similar) so
the sweep knows what still needs sending.

### 2. Silent misconfiguration in `notification_level`
No crash, no error — a level gets set wrong (or a producer passes the
wrong id) and something important is quietly treated as low-priority.

*Mitigation:* a floor on certain sources (e.g. `source = 'audit'`
can't resolve below a minimum level) enforced in `create_message()`'s
logic, not just left to lookup-table content. Carried over from the
Messages schema doc as an open decision.

### 3. Dispatch failure that never surfaces
The listener calls Apprise; Apprise's own call to Telegram/SMTP/SMS
can fail (expired token, SMTP auth lapsed, rate limit) with nothing in
the chain checking or surfacing that failure.

*Mitigation:* the listener treats an Apprise failure response as its
own failure (non-zero exit, not log-and-continue), so systemd's
`OnFailure=` can chain to a separate escalation unit — one that
notifies through an independent path, ideally not routed through
Apprise itself, so an Apprise-specific outage doesn't also silence its
own failure alert. journald captures the crash/restart trail for
after-the-fact forensics regardless.

### 4. Alert storms / lack of aggregation
A real incident (repeated failed logins) could fire the trigger
hundreds of times in a burst, each independently notifying — a wall of
pings instead of one useful summary.

*Mitigation:* debouncing/aggregation decided at the trigger or listener
level (don't re-fire for the same pattern within N minutes) — this is
an application-logic decision, not something infrastructure solves.
Left as an explicit open question for whoever writes the audit
trigger, not silently deferred.

### 5. Partial availability — notified but unreachable
The listener and Apprise don't depend on Curator's web process at all,
so someone can be pinged "you have a message" while Curator itself is
down (deploy, crash, reboot) and have nowhere to actually read it yet.

*Mitigation:* not a bug to fix so much as a known gap to document —
notify-success doesn't imply read-access-success. `Restart=always` on
Curator's own unit shrinks the downtime window but doesn't eliminate
it.

### 6. Drift between producers and the `create_message()` contract
Same class of problem already seen elsewhere in this project (the
`steward` repo's on-disk SQL drifting from what's live in `wcyj`). If
`create_message()`'s signature or the `notification_level` values
change, a producer not updated in lockstep can silently pass a
malformed or stale payload.

*Mitigation:* no systemd or infrastructure fix applies here — this is
a coordination/versioning discipline problem, addressed the same way
the project already addresses SQL drift: confirm live behavior before
assuming producers match the current contract, rather than trusting
that everything was updated together.

---

## What systemd can and can't do here

Useful for: **1** (partially — narrows the window, doesn't close it),
**3** (meaningfully — `OnFailure=` gives a real escalation path), **5**
(partially — faster recovery, not elimination).

No help for: **2**, **4**, **6** — these are logic/configuration/
coordination failures, not process-liveness failures, and systemd has
no visibility into any of them.

`StartLimitIntervalSec=`/`StartLimitBurst=` on the listener's unit is
worth setting regardless, so a genuine crash-loop doesn't also become
an alert-loop — and systemd giving up entirely after repeated restart
failures is arguably the one state that most deserves its own loud,
one-time notification, since that's also the point where the
reconciliation sweep (mitigation for #1) has likely stopped running
too.

---

## Open questions

1. Where does "notification sent" get recorded — a column on
   `messages.messages`, or a separate log table? Needed either way for
   the reconciliation sweep in #1 to function.
2. Does the independent fallback channel for #3 exist yet, or is this
   the point where a second, Apprise-independent notification path
   (e.g. a carrier SMS gateway hit directly) gets scoped as its own
   small piece of work?
3. Debouncing logic for #4 — trigger-level (Postgres) or listener-level
   (Python)? Affects where the "have I already alerted on this pattern
   recently" state lives.

## 📄 tasks.py

"""Task routes — CRUD for projects.tasks via api.save_task /
api.delete_task.

Mirrors contacts.py/organizations.py's structure exactly — same
deps.py helpers, same route shapes, same save/delete error contract.
Tasks have no "name" field (they use "description" instead), so the
blank-field guard is a local check rather than deps.py's require_name()
— see _require_description() below.
"""

import json

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from dbkit.connection import AsyncDBConnection
from curator.web.deps import (
    get_db,
    call_proc_and_refetch,
    delete_via_proc,
    get_detail_or_404,
    get_user_id,
    _fetch_json_scalar,
)

router = APIRouter()


async def _fetch_task_for_display(db: AsyncDBConnection, task_id: int) -> dict:
    """Fetch a task via api.get_task_detail() for the detail panel.

    Returns dict with id, project_id, parent_id, description, notes,
    status_id, priority_id keys — matches projects.v_task_detail's
    whitelist — or None if not found.
    """
    return await _fetch_json_scalar(
        db, "SELECT api.get_task_detail(%s)", (task_id,)
    )


def _require_description(description: str):
    """Return a rejection response if description is blank, else None.

    Tasks don't have a "name" field — deps.py's require_name() is
    name-specific in both the field it checks and its message text, so
    this is a small local equivalent rather than a forced reuse. If a
    third entity ever needs the same "required text field, different
    name" shape, that's the point to extract a generic version into
    deps.py — two occurrences doesn't yet justify it.

    NOTE — this is a cheap early-exit for the single most common blank
    submission, not a complete mirror of api.save_task()'s validation.
    Confirmed against the live function body (2026-07-10):
    api.save_task() itself also rejects a missing/null project_id
    ("A project is required.") and a missing/null status_id ("Task
    status is required."), each returning its own
    {"success": false, ...} envelope. Those two are deliberately NOT
    re-checked here — project_id always arrives via the hidden field
    (set from context, never user-typed, so effectively always
    present), and status_id's presence depends on the form having a
    sensible default value (see the default-status discussion —
    unresolved as of this changedoc). This function only exists to
    save a round trip on the one rejection a person can trivially
    cause themselves (leaving description blank); the proc remains the
    real authority for project_id/status_id, and call_proc_and_refetch
    already forwards its rejection message straight through to the UI
    if either is somehow missing.
    """
    if not description:
        return JSONResponse({
            "success": False,
            "message": "Description is required.",
            "data": None,
        })
    return None


# -- Single task fetch (for detail panel) -------------------------------------

@router.get("/crew/tasks/{task_id}")
async def get_task(
    task_id: int,
    db: AsyncDBConnection = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Fetch a single task as JSON for the detail panel."""
    return await get_detail_or_404(
        db, _fetch_task_for_display, task_id, "Task not found"
    )


# -- Task save routes ----------------------------------------------------------
# /crew/tasks/save must be declared before /crew/tasks/{task_id}/save to
# prevent "save" matching as a task_id integer.

@router.post("/crew/tasks/save")
async def save_new_task(
    request: Request,
    db: AsyncDBConnection = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Insert a new task via api.save_task().

    Accepts JSON body: {description, notes, status_id, priority_id,
    project_id, parent_id}. project_id arrives from the form's hidden
    field (pre-filled by panel.py's panel_new() from the ?project_id=
    query param — see nested_master_detail_design.md). parent_id is
    '' for a top-level task.

    Returns the new task record as JSON on success (200).
    Returns {"success": false, "message": "...", "data": ...} (200) on
    failure. api.save_task() enforces, in order: description required,
    project_id required and must reference an existing project,

## File 1 — `fieldkit_overrides.yaml`

### BEFORE

```yaml
projects.v_project_detail:
  type_id:
    control: select
    label: Type
    source: project_types
  status_id:
    control: select
    label: Status
    source: project_statuses
```

### AFTER

```yaml
projects.v_project_detail:
  type_id:
    control: select
    label: Type
    source: project_types
  status_id:
    control: select
    label: Status
    source: project_statuses

projects.v_task_detail:
  project_id:
    control: hidden
    # Pre-filled from context (the parent Project) via the query param
    # panel_new() forwards into the record dict — e.g.
    # /panel/tasks/new?project_id=12. Never user-editable; a subtask's
    # panel always opens from its parent task/project, never a bare
    # form the person fills in project_id on themselves.
  parent_id:
    control: hidden
    # Same reasoning as project_id. Empty ('') for a top-level task.
    # Subtask creation (pre-filling parent_id from the parent task) is
    # part of the Subtasks feature — deferred, see
    # nested_master_detail_design.md's "Deferred" section.
  status_id:
    control: select
    label: Status
    source: task_statuses
  priority_id:
    control: select
    label: Priority
    source: priorities
```

### Why

- `project_id`/`parent_id` are `*_id` columns on `v_task_detail`, so
  fieldkit requires an override entry for both regardless — this
  satisfies that requirement while also declaring them `hidden`, per
  the nested master-detail design's hidden-field-plus-context-line
  approach.
- `status_id`/`priority_id` use the `task_statuses`/`priorities`
  lookup sources — both already added to `api.get_lookup()` in the
  2026-07-08 Tasks SQL layer changedoc, so no SQL work needed here.

### AFTER

```html
{% for field in fields %}
  {% if field.field_type == "hidden" %}
    {# No wrapping .form-group / label / help_text — a hidden field has
       nothing to display. Rendering the bare <input type="hidden">
       still submits it as part of the form's FormData, which is all
       it needs to do. #}
    <input
      type="hidden"
      id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
      name="{{ field.name }}"
      value="{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}"
    />

  {% else %}
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="detail-{{ field.name }}">{{ field.label }}</label>

      {% if field.field_type == "text" %}
        <input
          type="text"
          id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
          name="{{ field.name }}"
          value="{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}"
          {% if field.placeholder %}placeholder="{{ field.placeholder }}"{% endif %}
        />

      {% elif field.field_type == "textarea" %}
        <textarea
          id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
          name="{{ field.name }}"
          {% if field.placeholder %}placeholder="{{ field.placeholder }}"{% endif %}
        >{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}</textarea>

      {% elif field.field_type == "select" %}
        <select id="detail-{{ field.name }}" name="{{ field.name }}">
          <option value="">—</option>
          {% for opt in options.get(field.source, []) %}
            <option
              value="{{ opt.value }}"
              {% if record.get(field.name) == opt.value %}selected{% endif %}
            >
              {{ opt.label }}
            </option>
          {% endfor %}
        </select>

      {% elif field.field_type == "date" %}
        <input
          type="date"
          id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
          name="{{ field.name }}"
          value="{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}"
        />

      {% elif field.field_type == "checkbox" %}
        <input
          type="checkbox"
          id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
          name="{{ field.name }}"
          {% if record.get(field.name) %}checked{% endif %}
        />
      {% endif %}

      {% if field.help_text %}
        <small class="form-help">{{ field.help_text }}</small>
      {% endif %}
    </div>
  {% endif %}
{% endfor %}
```

### Why

- Every existing field type keeps its exact current markup — the
  `{% else %}` branch is a verbatim copy of the original loop body,
  just re-indented one level deeper.
- `hidden` fields skip the `.form-group`/`<label>`/`help_text` wrapper
  entirely, since there's nothing to label or explain — they exist
  purely to carry a value through `FormData` on save.
- Reads `record.get(field.name)` exactly like every other field type —
  no special-casing needed for the pre-fill-from-query-param behavior;
  it works automatically because `panel_new()` (below) puts the query
  param value into the same `record` dict this template already reads
  from.

```python
@router.get("/panel/{entity}/new")
async def panel_new(entity: str, request: Request):
    """Render the full panel content for a new, empty record."""
    if entity not in _FETCH_FUNCTIONS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail=f"Unknown entity: {entity}")
    return _render_panel_content(request, entity, {}, "")
```

### AFTER

```python
_FETCH_FUNCTIONS = {
    "projects": _fetch_project_for_display,
    "contacts": _fetch_contact_for_display,
    "organizations": _fetch_organization_for_display,
    "tasks": _fetch_task_for_display,
}
```

```python
@router.get("/panel/{entity}/new")
async def panel_new(entity: str, request: Request):
    """Render the full panel content for a new, empty record.

    Any query parameters on the request are forwarded into the record
    dict verbatim — e.g. /panel/tasks/new?project_id=12 pre-fills the
    Tasks form's hidden project_id field with '12'. This is the only
    mechanism for prefilling a new-record panel; it stays entity-
    agnostic on purpose (panel.py never checks entity to decide which
    query params are meaningful — that's fieldkit_overrides.yaml's
    job, via which fields exist and are marked hidden). A query param
    with no matching field name is simply ignored by
    _detail_form_fields.html's record.get(field.name) lookups.
    """
    if entity not in _FETCH_FUNCTIONS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail=f"Unknown entity: {entity}")
    record = dict(request.query_params)
    return _render_panel_content(request, entity, record, "")
```

Also add the import (alongside the three existing `_fetch_*_for_display`
imports near the top of the file):

### BEFORE

```python
from curator.web.routes.contacts import _fetch_contact_for_display
from curator.web.routes.organizations import _fetch_organization_for_display
from curator.web.routes.projects import _fetch_project_for_display
```

### AFTER

```python
from curator.web.routes.contacts import _fetch_contact_for_display
from curator.web.routes.organizations import _fetch_organization_for_display
from curator.web.routes.projects import _fetch_project_for_display
from curator.web.routes.tasks import _fetch_task_for_display
```

### Why

- `dict(request.query_params)` — FastAPI's `Request.query_params` is a
  `Starlette` `QueryParams` (multidict-like) object; converting to a
  plain `dict` keeps only the last value per key, which is fine here
  since every current use case (a single parent id) never repeats a key.
- Deliberately generic: no `if entity == "tasks": ...` branching. Any
  future entity needing a pre-filled hidden field on its new-record
  panel gets this for free, the same way fieldkit's schema
  introspection already works for any entity without per-entity code.

## File 4 — `tasks.py` (new file)

```python
"""Task routes — CRUD for projects.tasks via api.save_task /
api.delete_task.

Mirrors contacts.py/organizations.py's structure exactly — same
deps.py helpers, same route shapes, same save/delete error contract.
Tasks have no "name" field (they use "description" instead), so the
blank-field guard is a local check rather than deps.py's require_name()
— see _require_description() below.
"""

import json

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, Request
from dbkit.connection import AsyncDBConnection
from curator.web.deps import (
    get_db,
    call_proc_and_refetch,
    delete_via_proc,
    get_detail_or_404,
    get_user_id,
    _fetch_json_scalar,
)
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

router = APIRouter()


async def _fetch_task_for_display(db: AsyncDBConnection, task_id: int) -> dict:
    """Fetch a task via api.get_task_detail() for the detail panel.

    Returns dict with id, project_id, parent_id, description, notes,
    status_id, priority_id keys — matches projects.v_task_detail's
    whitelist — or None if not found.
    """
    return await _fetch_json_scalar(
        db, "SELECT api.get_task_detail(%s)", (task_id,)
    )


def _require_description(description: str):
    """Return a rejection response if description is blank, else None.

    Tasks don't have a "name" field — deps.py's require_name() is
    name-specific in both the field it checks and its message text, so
    this is a small local equivalent rather than a forced reuse. If a
    third entity ever needs the same "required text field, different
    name" shape, that's the point to extract a generic version into
    deps.py — two occurrences doesn't yet justify it.

    NOTE — this is a cheap early-exit for the single most common blank
    submission, not a complete mirror of api.save_task()'s validation.
    Confirmed against the live function body (2026-07-10):
    api.save_task() itself also rejects a missing/null project_id
    ("A project is required.") and a missing/null status_id ("Task
    status is required."), each returning its own
    {"success": false, ...} envelope. Those two are deliberately NOT
    re-checked here — project_id always arrives via the hidden field
    (set from context, never user-typed, so effectively always
    present), and status_id's presence depends on the form having a
    sensible default value (see the default-status discussion —
    unresolved as of this changedoc). This function only exists to
    save a round trip on the one rejection a person can trivially
    cause themselves (leaving description blank); the proc remains the
    real authority for project_id/status_id, and call_proc_and_refetch
    already forwards its rejection message straight through to the UI
    if either is somehow missing.
    """
    if not description:
        return JSONResponse({
            "success": False,
            "message": "Description is required.",
            "data": None,
        })
    return None


# -- Single task fetch (for detail panel) -------------------------------------

@router.get("/crew/tasks/{task_id}")
async def get_task(
    task_id: int,
    db: AsyncDBConnection = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Fetch a single task as JSON for the detail panel."""
    return await get_detail_or_404(
        db, _fetch_task_for_display, task_id, "Task not found"
    )


# -- Task save routes ----------------------------------------------------------
# /crew/tasks/save must be declared before /crew/tasks/{task_id}/save to
# prevent "save" matching as a task_id integer.

@router.post("/crew/tasks/save")
async def save_new_task(
    request: Request,
    db: AsyncDBConnection = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Insert a new task via api.save_task().

    Accepts JSON body: {description, notes, status_id, priority_id,
    project_id, parent_id}. project_id arrives from the form's hidden
    field (pre-filled by panel.py's panel_new() from the ?project_id=
    query param — see nested_master_detail_design.md). parent_id is
    '' for a top-level task.

    Returns the new task record as JSON on success (200).
    Returns {"success": false, "message": "...", "data": ...} (200) on
    failure. api.save_task() enforces, in order: description required,
    project_id required and must reference an existing project,
    status_id required and must reference an existing task_status,
    parent_id (if given) must belong to the same project and not equal
    the task's own id. Only the description check is duplicated in
    Python (see _require_description) — the rest are the proc's alone.
    """
    body = await request.json()
    description = (body.get("description") or "").strip()
    notes = body.get("notes") or None
    status_id = body.get("status_id") or None
    priority_id = body.get("priority_id") or None
    project_id = body.get("project_id") or None
    parent_id = body.get("parent_id") or None

    rejection = _require_description(description)
    if rejection:
        return rejection

    user_id = get_user_id(request)

    payload = {
        "description": description,
        "notes": notes,
        "status_id": status_id,
        "priority_id": priority_id,
        "project_id": project_id,
        "parent_id": parent_id,
    }

    return await call_proc_and_refetch(
        db,
        "SELECT api.save_task(%s, %s)",
        (json.dumps(payload), user_id),
        _fetch_task_for_display,
        None,
        "Insert succeeded but fetch failed",
    )


@router.post("/crew/tasks/{task_id}/save")
async def save_task(
    task_id: int,
    request: Request,
    db: AsyncDBConnection = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Save edits to an existing task via api.save_task().

    Accepts JSON body: {description, notes, status_id, priority_id,
    project_id, parent_id}.

    Returns the updated task record as JSON on success (200).
    Returns {"success": false, "message": "...", "data": ...} (200) on
    failure — task not found, plus the same description/project_id/
    status_id/parent_id validation api.save_task() enforces on insert
    (see save_new_task's docstring above for the full list).
    """
    body = await request.json()
    description = (body.get("description") or "").strip()
    notes = body.get("notes") or None
    status_id = body.get("status_id") or None
    priority_id = body.get("priority_id") or None
    project_id = body.get("project_id") or None
    parent_id = body.get("parent_id") or None

    rejection = _require_description(description)
    if rejection:
        return rejection

    user_id = get_user_id(request)

    payload = {
        "id": task_id,
        "description": description,
        "notes": notes,
        "status_id": status_id,
        "priority_id": priority_id,
        "project_id": project_id,
        "parent_id": parent_id,
    }

    return await call_proc_and_refetch(
        db,
        "SELECT api.save_task(%s, %s)",
        (json.dumps(payload), user_id),
        _fetch_task_for_display,
        task_id,
        "Save succeeded but fetch failed",
    )


@router.delete("/crew/tasks/{task_id}")
async def delete_task(
    task_id: int,
    request: Request,
    db: AsyncDBConnection = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Delete a task by id via api.delete_task().

    Returns 204 No Content on success.
    Returns {"success": false, "message": "..."} (200) on failure —
    e.g. not found, or blocked by undeleted child tasks (per
    api.delete_task()'s explicit child-task detection,
    CHANGEDOC_TASKS_SQL_LAYER.md).
    """
    user_id = get_user_id(request)
    return await delete_via_proc(
        db, "SELECT api.delete_task(%s, %s)", (task_id, user_id)
    )
```

### Why

- Structurally identical to `contacts.py`/`organizations.py` — same
  `deps.py` helpers (`call_proc_and_refetch`, `delete_via_proc`,
  `get_detail_or_404`, `get_user_id`), same route-ordering rule
  (literal `/save` before `/{id}/save}`), same error contract. This was
  explicitly verified in the datasheet URL-fix session (2026-07-10) —
  every entity's save/delete goes through the same shared helpers, so
  Tasks needed no special-casing to match.
- `_require_description()` is a small local function rather than
  forcing tasks to use `deps.py`'s `require_name()`, which is
  name-specific in both field and message wording. Flagged in its own
  docstring as a two-occurrences-isn't-a-pattern-yet judgment call —
  worth revisiting if a third entity needs the same shape.
- `status_id`/`priority_id`/`project_id`/`parent_id` are passed through
  as raw strings from the JSON body (or `None` if blank) without int
  casting — matches `projects.py`'s handling of `type_id`/`status_id`,
  which relies on psycopg/Postgres to compare a numeric-string against
  an integer column correctly.

```yaml
      FROM projects.tasks t
      LEFT JOIN projects.task_status ts ON ts.id = t.status_id
      LEFT JOIN projects.priority    p  ON p.id  = t.priority_id
      WHERE t.project_id = %s
        AND t.parent_id IS NULL
      ORDER BY t.created_at

  # Fetch sub-tasks for a parent task
  for_task:
    type: select_all
    sql: >
      SELECT
          t.id,
          t.description::text,
          t.notes::text,
          t.status_id,
          ts.name::text AS status,
          t.priority_id,
          p.name::text  AS priority,
          t.created_at::text
      FROM projects.tasks t
      LEFT JOIN projects.task_status ts ON ts.id = t.status_id
      LEFT JOIN projects.priority    p  ON p.id  = t.priority_id
      WHERE t.parent_id = %s
      ORDER BY t.created_at
```

### Why

- `t.sort_order` was dropped from `projects.tasks` in the Tasks SQL
  layer changedoc (2026-07-08) — both queries still selected and
  ordered by it, which would error the moment either query actually
  ran. Removed the column from the `SELECT` list and the `ORDER BY`
  clause in both.
- Ordering falls back to `t.created_at` — matches your stated
  intention ("ordering by naming convention or sort-by-name/date in
  the UI") until/unless a naming-convention-based sort is added at the
  UI layer later.

```python
from curator.web.routes import auth, landing, crew, panel, projects, contacts, organizations

_FIELDKIT_VIEWS = {
```

```python
app.include_router(auth.router)
```

### AFTER

```python
from curator.web.routes import (
    auth, landing, crew, panel, projects, contacts, organizations, tasks,
)

_FIELDKIT_VIEWS = {
    "projects": "projects.v_project_detail",
    "contacts": "identity.v_contact_detail",
    "organizations": "identity.v_organization_detail",

}
```

```python
app.include_router(auth.router)
app.include_router(landing.router)
app.include_router(crew.router)
app.include_router(panel.router)
app.include_router(projects.router)
app.include_router(contacts.router)

app.include_router(tasks.router)
```

### Why

- `_FIELDKIT_VIEWS` entry lets `FieldKit.create()` build the Tasks
  cache at startup, same as every other entity — this is also where
  the `hidden`-type `FieldDef`s for `project_id`/`parent_id` actually
  get constructed and validated (via `fieldkit_overrides.yaml`'s new
  entries), so a mistake in that YAML (wrong source name, etc.) will
  crash uvicorn at startup exactly as designed, not surface as a broken
  form later.
- Router registration follows the same pattern as every other entity —
  no special treatment.

## 📄 function_export_tool_design

# Design Doc — `api` Schema Function Export Tool

**Status:** Parked. Not scheduled — captured so the idea and the
review notes aren't lost before it's picked up.

## Problem

The `steward` repo's numbered `.sql` files (`06b_api_projects.sql`,
`06c_api_identity.sql`, etc.) have drifted out of sync with what's
actually live in `wcyj` — confirmed directly during Tasks UI wiring
(2026-07-10): `06b_api_projects.sql` doesn't contain `api.save_task()`
or `api.delete_task()` at all, even though both exist and work in the
live database. This is already a flagged gap from the 2026-07-08
handoff ("steward repo `.sql` files may be out of sync").

Separately, having each `api.*` function in its own file (rather than
only inside the large numbered files) would make it easier to:
- see at a glance everything that exists in `api.*`
- spot functions written for one entity that could be reused or
  patterned after for another
- diff a single function's history in git, rather than diffing a
  1000+-line numbered file every time one function changes

## Direction decided (2026-07-10)

This is a **documentation tool**, not a migration/DevOps tool —
`pgschema` (https://github.com/pgplex/pgschema, actively maintained,
Apache-2.0, Terraform-style declarative schema migration) was
evaluated and ruled out for this purpose: its dump step is oriented
around producing one consolidated, hand-editable `schema.sql` for a
plan/apply migration workflow, not one clean file per function for
browsing/reuse-spotting/diffing. Adopting it would mean taking on its
whole opinionated migration workflow for a feature (extraction) that's
a side effect of its actual purpose, not its core design.

`pg_extractor` remains the right direction — narrower in scope, closer
to the original need, permissively licensed, worth forking and
patching for current Postgres compatibility (see below).

**New idea, worth pursuing together:** integrate the forked
`pg_extractor` output with the existing "Dr. Filewalker" Project Crew
member (Carolyn's doc-gen package that walks a repo and produces
syntax-highlighted code documentation). Rather than the fork producing
a standalone folder of `.sql` files as its own separate artifact,
structure its output so Dr. Filewalker's existing walker picks up the
per-function files as just another set of source files in the tree —
giving `api.*` functions the same syntax-highlighted, browsable
treatment as the rest of the codebase, in the same place, rather than
a second disconnected place to remember to look. Open question when
this is picked up: does Dr. Filewalker walk a single repo tree today,
or would it need to pull from two sources (the repo tree, plus a
live-DB extraction step) as part of one run? That's the one piece of
new plumbing this idea actually needs — the fork's job is getting the
file naming/structure right so the handoff is clean, not building a
second presentation layer.

## Prior art — evaluate before building

Before writing a custom tool, check existing options:

- **`pg_extractor`** (https://github.com/omniti-labs/pg_extractor) —
  closest match to this need; purpose-built for dumping schema objects
  (including functions) to individual files with naming/directory
  conventions already worked out. Last commit ~5 years old as of
  2026-07-10. Licensed under the PostgreSQL License (permissive,
  BSD/MIT-equivalent, confirmed 2026-07-10) — no friction to fork,
  patch for current Postgres compatibility, and republish under the
  same license. Plan: fork, identify what's actually broken against a
  current Postgres version (likely candidates: renamed/shifted
  pg_catalog columns across major versions, deprecated pg_dump/psql
  flags, possible Python version drift if it's Python-based), fix, and
  either PR back to the original repo (worth trying even on a
  long-quiet repo) or maintain independently if it's abandoned for
  good.
- **`pglast`** (Postgres SQL parser via `libpg_query`) — solves a
  different problem (programmatic SQL analysis/transformation, not
  extraction-to-files). Not a fit for this specific need, but worth
  keeping in mind for potential future use (e.g. validating
  `queries.yaml`'s SQL syntactically before it hits the database).

## Starting point

A script (not originally written for this project) that uses
`pg_get_functiondef()` to export each function in a schema to its own
`.sql` file. The mechanism is sound — `pg_get_functiondef()` returns
a complete, correctly-delimited `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ...`
statement, which is much more reliable than trying to slice a
`pg_dump` schema dump apart by hand (e.g. via `awk` boundary-matching
on `$$;`, which is fragile the moment delimiter style isn't perfectly
consistent).

## Required changes before use in this project

1. **Connection config must go through `dbkit`, not raw
   `psycopg`/hardcoded credentials.** The original script's
   `DB_CONFIG` dict hardcodes `dbname`/`user`/`password`/`host`/`port`
   as literals — directly against this project's own convention
   (passwords in `~/.pgpass`, connection params in
   `~/.config/dev-utils/config.yaml`, never in code). Fix: use
   `dbkit.connection.DBConnection` directly instead of raw `psycopg`:

   ```python
   from dbkit.connection import DBConnection

   with DBConnection() as db:
       rows = db.fetch_all(
           """
           SELECT p.proname, pg_get_functiondef(p.oid)
           FROM pg_proc p
           JOIN pg_namespace n ON p.pronamespace = n.oid
           WHERE n.nspname = %s AND p.prokind = %s
           """,
           (SCHEMA_NAME, ...),
       )
   ```

   This also makes the script portable to any machine with
   `~/.pgpass`/`config.yaml` already set up, rather than tied to one
   hardcoded host.

2. **`prokind` filter should account for procedures, not just
   functions.** The original only selects `prokind = 'f'`. Every
   `api.*` object confirmed so far (`save_task`, `save_project`,
   `get_task_detail`, etc.) is a `FUNCTION`, so this is correct today
   — but if a real `PROCEDURE` (`prokind = 'p'`) is ever added to
   `api.*`, this filter would silently skip exporting it. Fix: either
   `prokind IN ('f', 'p')` from the start, or a code comment
   documenting the current all-functions assumption so a future
   `CREATE PROCEDURE` doesn't go missing from the export without
   anyone noticing.

3. **Overloaded functions would silently collide on filename.** Every
   function name in `api.*` is currently unique, so `{func_name}.sql`
   is safe as-is. If two functions ever share a name with different
   signatures, the second export would silently overwrite the first
   with no warning. Fix: use `pg_get_function_identity_arguments(p.oid)`
   to build a signature-qualified filename whenever more than one
   function shares a name (e.g. `save_task__jsonb_bigint.sql`), falling
   back to the plain name when there's no collision.

## Open question — where does this tool live?

This is a generic "dump any Postgres schema's functions to individual
files" utility, not specific to Curator's business logic. It likely
belongs alongside `dbkit`/`viewkit` in the `dev-utils` repo (as its own
small script or CLI entry point) rather than inside the `curator` repo
— consistent with `dbkit`/`viewkit` already being the home for
reusable, non-Curator-specific infrastructure. Not decided; revisit
when this is actually built.

## Open question — does this replace or supplement the numbered files?

Two different things this tool could produce, worth deciding
separately when it's actually built:

- **A reconciliation snapshot** — run once, diff by eye against
  `06b_api_projects.sql`/`06c_api_identity.sql`/etc., then manually
  update those numbered files to match reality. One-time use of the
  tool's output, not an ongoing artifact.
- **An ongoing parallel structure** — `.../api/functions/*.sql` living
  permanently alongside the numbered files, kept in sync going forward
  (e.g. regenerated after any Tasks-SQL-layer-style change). This adds
  a second place that needs updating every time a function changes —
  worth weighing against the "one canonical implementation" principle
  already applied elsewhere in this project (e.g. `_detail_panel_content.html`
  as the only panel renderer, `datasheet.js` as the only child-datasheet
  engine) before committing to it as a permanent parallel structure
  rather than a one-off tool.

## Not scoped yet

- Exact output directory structure (`steward/databases/wcyj/api/` vs.
  `scripts/` vs. something else) — Carolyn mentioned both `.../data`
  (seed files) and `.../sql` (numbered files) as existing conventions
  in the `steward` repo; where a new per-function folder fits alongside
  those isn't decided.
- Whether this becomes a one-off script or a proper CLI tool with
  options (schema name, output dir, dry-run, etc.).
- Any templating/header convention for the exported files (e.g. a
  comment noting "auto-generated, do not hand-edit — regenerate from
  wcyj" at the top of each file, to avoid someone editing the export
  and having it silently diverge from the live database again).

## 📄 CHANGEDOC_TASKS_UI_WIRING_BACKEND

# CHANGEDOC — Tasks UI Wiring: Backend Pieces

**Status:** Ready to apply. Requires the viewkit `hidden` field_type
change (CHANGEDOC_VIEWKIT_HIDDEN_FIELD_TYPE.md) already applied and
reinstalled — confirmed done 2026-07-10.

**Payload shape verified 2026-07-10** against `api.save_task()`'s live
`prosrc` in `wcyj` (pulled via pgAdmin — the on-disk copy of
`06b_api_projects.sql` is stale and doesn't contain the Tasks functions
at all; a doc-sync gap, flagged separately). `tasks.py`'s payload keys
and the `_require_description` guard are accurate against what the
database actually enforces, not just the 2026-07-08 handoff's prose
summary.

**Not included here:** the nested master-detail Tasks tab layout
itself (Tabulator list + nested form in `_detail_panel_content.html`)
and the `detail-panel.js` multi-panel refactor it depends on. Those are
separate, larger pieces — this changedoc only gets Tasks to the point
where `/panel/tasks/{id}`, `/panel/tasks/new`, and `/crew/tasks/...`
all work correctly on their own, testable independently of any UI that
calls them yet.

## Summary of changes

1. `fieldkit_overrides.yaml` — new `projects.v_task_detail` entry
2. `_detail_form_fields.html` — new `hidden` field_type render branch
3. `panel.py` — `panel_new()` now forwards query params into the
   (empty) record dict, so a hidden field can be pre-filled on a new
   record via e.g. `/panel/tasks/new?project_id=12`; `tasks` added to
   `_FETCH_FUNCTIONS`
4. `tasks.py` — new route file, mirrors `contacts.py`/`organizations.py`
   exactly
5. `queries.yaml` — `tasks.for_project`/`tasks.for_task`: drop stale
   `ORDER BY t.sort_order` (column no longer exists)
6. `app.py` — `tasks` added to `_FIELDKIT_VIEWS`, `tasks` router
   registered

## File 1 — `fieldkit_overrides.yaml`

### BEFORE

```yaml
projects.v_project_detail:
  type_id:
    control: select
    label: Type
    source: project_types
  status_id:
    control: select
    label: Status
    source: project_statuses
```

### AFTER

```yaml
projects.v_project_detail:
  type_id:
    control: select
    label: Type
    source: project_types
  status_id:
    control: select
    label: Status
    source: project_statuses

projects.v_task_detail:
  project_id:
    control: hidden
    # Pre-filled from context (the parent Project) via the query param
    # panel_new() forwards into the record dict — e.g.
    # /panel/tasks/new?project_id=12. Never user-editable; a subtask's
    # panel always opens from its parent task/project, never a bare
    # form the person fills in project_id on themselves.
  parent_id:
    control: hidden
    # Same reasoning as project_id. Empty ('') for a top-level task.
    # Subtask creation (pre-filling parent_id from the parent task) is
    # part of the Subtasks feature — deferred, see
    # nested_master_detail_design.md's "Deferred" section.
  status_id:
    control: select
    label: Status
    source: task_statuses
  priority_id:
    control: select
    label: Priority
    source: priorities
```

### Why

- `project_id`/`parent_id` are `*_id` columns on `v_task_detail`, so
  fieldkit requires an override entry for both regardless — this
  satisfies that requirement while also declaring them `hidden`, per
  the nested master-detail design's hidden-field-plus-context-line
  approach.
- `status_id`/`priority_id` use the `task_statuses`/`priorities`
  lookup sources — both already added to `api.get_lookup()` in the
  2026-07-08 Tasks SQL layer changedoc, so no SQL work needed here.

---

## File 2 — `_detail_form_fields.html`

### BEFORE

```html
{% for field in fields %}
  <div class="form-group">
    <label for="detail-{{ field.name }}">{{ field.label }}</label>

    {% if field.field_type == "text" %}
      <input
        type="text"
        id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
        name="{{ field.name }}"
        value="{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}"
        {% if field.placeholder %}placeholder="{{ field.placeholder }}"{% endif %}
      />

    {% elif field.field_type == "textarea" %}
      <textarea
        id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
        name="{{ field.name }}"
        {% if field.placeholder %}placeholder="{{ field.placeholder }}"{% endif %}
      >{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}</textarea>

    {% elif field.field_type == "select" %}
      <select id="detail-{{ field.name }}" name="{{ field.name }}">
        <option value="">—</option>
        {% for opt in options.get(field.source, []) %}
          <option
            value="{{ opt.value }}"
            {% if record.get(field.name) == opt.value %}selected{% endif %}
          >
            {{ opt.label }}
          </option>
        {% endfor %}
      </select>

    {% elif field.field_type == "date" %}
      <input
        type="date"
        id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
        name="{{ field.name }}"
        value="{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}"
      />

    {% elif field.field_type == "checkbox" %}
      <input
        type="checkbox"
        id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
        name="{{ field.name }}"
        {% if record.get(field.name) %}checked{% endif %}
      />
    {% endif %}

    {% if field.help_text %}
      <small class="form-help">{{ field.help_text }}</small>
    {% endif %}
  </div>
{% endfor %}
```

### AFTER

```html
{% for field in fields %}
  {% if field.field_type == "hidden" %}
    {# No wrapping .form-group / label / help_text — a hidden field has
       nothing to display. Rendering the bare <input type="hidden">
       still submits it as part of the form's FormData, which is all
       it needs to do. #}
    <input
      type="hidden"
      id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
      name="{{ field.name }}"
      value="{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}"
    />

  {% else %}
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="detail-{{ field.name }}">{{ field.label }}</label>

      {% if field.field_type == "text" %}
        <input
          type="text"
          id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
          name="{{ field.name }}"
          value="{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}"
          {% if field.placeholder %}placeholder="{{ field.placeholder }}"{% endif %}
        />

      {% elif field.field_type == "textarea" %}
        <textarea
          id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
          name="{{ field.name }}"
          {% if field.placeholder %}placeholder="{{ field.placeholder }}"{% endif %}
        >{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}</textarea>

      {% elif field.field_type == "select" %}
        <select id="detail-{{ field.name }}" name="{{ field.name }}">
          <option value="">—</option>
          {% for opt in options.get(field.source, []) %}
            <option
              value="{{ opt.value }}"
              {% if record.get(field.name) == opt.value %}selected{% endif %}
            >
              {{ opt.label }}
            </option>
          {% endfor %}
        </select>

      {% elif field.field_type == "date" %}
        <input
          type="date"
          id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
          name="{{ field.name }}"
          value="{{ record.get(field.name) or '' }}"
        />

      {% elif field.field_type == "checkbox" %}
        <input
          type="checkbox"
          id="detail-{{ field.name }}"
          name="{{ field.name }}"
          {% if record.get(field.name) %}checked{% endif %}
        />
      {% endif %}

      {% if field.help_text %}
        <small class="form-help">{{ field.help_text }}</small>
      {% endif %}
    </div>
  {% endif %}
{% endfor %}
```

### Why

- Every existing field type keeps its exact current markup — the
  `{% else %}` branch is a verbatim copy of the original loop body,
  just re-indented one level deeper.
- `hidden` fields skip the `.form-group`/`<label>`/`help_text` wrapper
  entirely, since there's nothing to label or explain — they exist
  purely to carry a value through `FormData` on save.
- Reads `record.get(field.name)` exactly like every other field type —
  no special-casing needed for the pre-fill-from-query-param behavior;
  it works automatically because `panel_new()` (below) puts the query
  param value into the same `record` dict this template already reads
  from.

```python
    """Render the full panel content for a new, empty record."""

        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail=f"Unknown entity: {entity}")
```

### AFTER

```python

    "projects": _fetch_project_for_display,
    "contacts": _fetch_contact_for_display,
    "organizations": _fetch_organization_for_display,
    "tasks": _fetch_task_for_display,
```

```python
@router.get("/panel/{entity}/new")
async def panel_new(entity: str, request: Request):
    """Render the full panel content for a new, empty record.

    Any query parameters on the request are forwarded into the record
    dict verbatim — e.g. /panel/tasks/new?project_id=12 pre-fills the
    Tasks form's hidden project_id field with '12'. This is the only
    mechanism for prefilling a new-record panel; it stays entity-
    agnostic on purpose (panel.py never checks entity to decide which
    query params are meaningful — that's fieldkit_overrides.yaml's
    job, via which fields exist and are marked hidden). A query param
    with no matching field name is simply ignored by
    _detail_form_fields.html's record.get(field.name) lookups.
    """
    if entity not in _FETCH_FUNCTIONS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail=f"Unknown entity: {entity}")
    record = dict(request.query_params)
    return _render_panel_content(request, entity, record, "")
```

Also add the import (alongside the three existing `_fetch_*_for_display`
imports near the top of the file):

### BEFORE

```python
from curator.web.routes.contacts import _fetch_contact_for_display
from curator.web.routes.organizations import _fetch_organization_for_display
from curator.web.routes.projects import _fetch_project_for_display
```

### AFTER

```python
from curator.web.routes.contacts import _fetch_contact_for_display
from curator.web.routes.organizations import _fetch_organization_for_display
from curator.web.routes.projects import _fetch_project_for_display
from curator.web.routes.tasks import _fetch_task_for_display
```

### Why

- `dict(request.query_params)` — FastAPI's `Request.query_params` is a
  `Starlette` `QueryParams` (multidict-like) object; converting to a
  plain `dict` keeps only the last value per key, which is fine here
  since every current use case (a single parent id) never repeats a key.
- Deliberately generic: no `if entity == "tasks": ...` branching. Any
  future entity needing a pre-filled hidden field on its new-record
  panel gets this for free, the same way fieldkit's schema
  introspection already works for any entity without per-entity code.

## File 4 — `tasks.py` (new file)

```python
"""Task routes — CRUD for projects.tasks via api.save_task /
api.delete_task.

Mirrors contacts.py/organizations.py's structure exactly — same
deps.py helpers, same route shapes, same save/delete error contract.
Tasks have no "name" field (they use "description" instead), so the
blank-field guard is a local check rather than deps.py's require_name()
— see _require_description() below.
"""

import json

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, Request
from dbkit.connection import AsyncDBConnection
from curator.web.deps import (
    get_db,
    call_proc_and_refetch,
    delete_via_proc,
    get_detail_or_404,
    get_user_id,
    _fetch_json_scalar,
)
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

router = APIRouter()


async def _fetch_task_for_display(db: AsyncDBConnection, task_id: int) -> dict:
    """Fetch a task via api.get_task_detail() for the detail panel.

    Returns dict with id, project_id, parent_id, description, notes,
    status_id, priority_id keys — matches projects.v_task_detail's
    whitelist — or None if not found.
    """
    return await _fetch_json_scalar(
        db, "SELECT api.get_task_detail(%s)", (task_id,)
    )


def _require_description(description: str):
    """Return a rejection response if description is blank, else None.

    Tasks don't have a "name" field — deps.py's require_name() is
    name-specific in both the field it checks and its message text, so
    this is a small local equivalent rather than a forced reuse. If a
    third entity ever needs the same "required text field, different
    name" shape, that's the point to extract a generic version into
    deps.py — two occurrences doesn't yet justify it.

    NOTE — this is a cheap early-exit for the single most common blank
    submission, not a complete mirror of api.save_task()'s validation.
    Confirmed against the live function body (2026-07-10):
    api.save_task() itself also rejects a missing/null project_id
    ("A project is required.") and a missing/null status_id ("Task
    status is required."), each returning its own
    {"success": false, ...} envelope. Those two are deliberately NOT
    re-checked here — project_id always arrives via the hidden field
    (set from context, never user-typed, so effectively always
    present), and status_id's presence depends on the form having a
    sensible default value (see the default-status discussion —
    unresolved as of this changedoc). This function only exists to
    save a round trip on the one rejection a person can trivially
    cause themselves (leaving description blank); the proc remains the
    real authority for project_id/status_id, and call_proc_and_refetch
    already forwards its rejection message straight through to the UI
    if either is somehow missing.
    """
    if not description:
        return JSONResponse({
            "success": False,
            "message": "Description is required.",
            "data": None,
        })
    return None


# -- Single task fetch (for detail panel) -------------------------------------

@router.get("/crew/tasks/{task_id}")
async def get_task(
    task_id: int,
    db: AsyncDBConnection = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Fetch a single task as JSON for the detail panel."""
    return await get_detail_or_404(
        db, _fetch_task_for_display, task_id, "Task not found"
    )


# -- Task save routes ----------------------------------------------------------
# /crew/tasks/save must be declared before /crew/tasks/{task_id}/save to
# prevent "save" matching as a task_id integer.

@router.post("/crew/tasks/save")
async def save_new_task(
    request: Request,
    db: AsyncDBConnection = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Insert a new task via api.save_task().

    Accepts JSON body: {description, notes, status_id, priority_id,
    project_id, parent_id}. project_id arrives from the form's hidden
    field (pre-filled by panel.py's panel_new() from the ?project_id=
    query param — see nested_master_detail_design.md). parent_id is
    '' for a top-level task.

    Returns the new task record as JSON on success (200).
    Returns {"success": false, "message": "...", "data": ...} (200) on
    failure. api.save_task() enforces, in order: description required,
    project_id required and must reference an existing project,
    status_id required and must reference an existing task_status,
    parent_id (if given) must belong to the same project and not equal
    the task's own id. Only the description check is duplicated in
    Python (see _require_description) — the rest are the proc's alone.
    """
    body = await request.json()
    description = (body.get("description") or "").strip()
    notes = body.get("notes") or None
    status_id = body.get("status_id") or None
    priority_id = body.get("priority_id") or None
    project_id = body.get("project_id") or None
    parent_id = body.get("parent_id") or None

    rejection = _require_description(description)
    if rejection:
        return rejection

    user_id = get_user_id(request)

    payload = {
        "description": description,
        "notes": notes,
        "status_id": status_id,
        "priority_id": priority_id,
        "project_id": project_id,
        "parent_id": parent_id,
    }

    return await call_proc_and_refetch(
        db,
        "SELECT api.save_task(%s, %s)",
        (json.dumps(payload), user_id),
        _fetch_task_for_display,
        None,
        "Insert succeeded but fetch failed",
    )


@router.post("/crew/tasks/{task_id}/save")
async def save_task(
    task_id: int,
    request: Request,
    db: AsyncDBConnection = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Save edits to an existing task via api.save_task().

    Accepts JSON body: {description, notes, status_id, priority_id,
    project_id, parent_id}.

    Returns the updated task record as JSON on success (200).
    Returns {"success": false, "message": "...", "data": ...} (200) on
    failure — task not found, plus the same description/project_id/
    status_id/parent_id validation api.save_task() enforces on insert
    (see save_new_task's docstring above for the full list).
    """
    body = await request.json()
    description = (body.get("description") or "").strip()
    notes = body.get("notes") or None
    status_id = body.get("status_id") or None
    priority_id = body.get("priority_id") or None
    project_id = body.get("project_id") or None
    parent_id = body.get("parent_id") or None

    rejection = _require_description(description)
    if rejection:
        return rejection

    user_id = get_user_id(request)

    payload = {
        "id": task_id,
        "description": description,
        "notes": notes,
        "status_id": status_id,
        "priority_id": priority_id,
        "project_id": project_id,
        "parent_id": parent_id,
    }

    return await call_proc_and_refetch(
        db,
        "SELECT api.save_task(%s, %s)",
        (json.dumps(payload), user_id),
        _fetch_task_for_display,
        task_id,
        "Save succeeded but fetch failed",
    )


@router.delete("/crew/tasks/{task_id}")
async def delete_task(
    task_id: int,
    request: Request,
    db: AsyncDBConnection = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Delete a task by id via api.delete_task().

    Returns 204 No Content on success.
    Returns {"success": false, "message": "..."} (200) on failure —
    e.g. not found, or blocked by undeleted child tasks (per
    api.delete_task()'s explicit child-task detection,
    CHANGEDOC_TASKS_SQL_LAYER.md).
    """
    user_id = get_user_id(request)
    return await delete_via_proc(
        db, "SELECT api.delete_task(%s, %s)", (task_id, user_id)
    )
```

### Why

- Structurally identical to `contacts.py`/`organizations.py` — same
  `deps.py` helpers (`call_proc_and_refetch`, `delete_via_proc`,
  `get_detail_or_404`, `get_user_id`), same route-ordering rule
  (literal `/save` before `/{id}/save}`), same error contract. This was
  explicitly verified in the datasheet URL-fix session (2026-07-10) —
  every entity's save/delete goes through the same shared helpers, so
  Tasks needed no special-casing to match.
- `_require_description()` is a small local function rather than
  forcing tasks to use `deps.py`'s `require_name()`, which is
  name-specific in both field and message wording. Flagged in its own
  docstring as a two-occurrences-isn't-a-pattern-yet judgment call —
  worth revisiting if a third entity needs the same shape.
- `status_id`/`priority_id`/`project_id`/`parent_id` are passed through
  as raw strings from the JSON body (or `None` if blank) without int
  casting — matches `projects.py`'s handling of `type_id`/`status_id`,
  which relies on psycopg/Postgres to compare a numeric-string against
  an integer column correctly.


### Why

- `t.sort_order` was dropped from `projects.tasks` in the Tasks SQL
  layer changedoc (2026-07-08) — both queries still selected and
  ordered by it, which would error the moment either query actually
  ran. Removed the column from the `SELECT` list and the `ORDER BY`
  clause in both.
- Ordering falls back to `t.created_at` — matches your stated
  intention ("ordering by naming convention or sort-by-name/date in

## 📄 CHANGEDOC_VIEWKIT_HIDDEN_FIELD_TYPE

# CHANGEDOC — viewkit: Add `hidden` field_type to FieldDef

**Repo:** `dev-utils` (`~/projects/dev-utils/python/viewkit/`)
**Status:** Ready to apply. Requires reinstall into Curator's venv —
viewkit is a regular (non-editable) install there, confirmed via
`pip show viewkit` / `pip list -e` (2026-07-10).

## Summary

Curator's Tasks UI wiring needs a `hidden` field type in fieldkit's
generic field-rendering system, for `project_id`/`parent_id` on tasks —
FK columns that must be submitted with the form but never shown as an
editable control (see `nested_master_detail_design.md`). `FieldDef`'s
own `__post_init__` validates `field_type` against a fixed set that
doesn't include `hidden`, so constructing one currently raises
`ValueError` before this can be used anywhere.

This is a one-line change to the validation set in `viewkit.models`,
not a Curator-side change — `viewkit` is Carolyn's own `dev-utils`
package (Curator is currently its only consumer, but it was designed
for reuse), so the fix belongs in the shared package, not worked around
locally in Curator.

---

## File — `python/viewkit/models.py`

### BEFORE

```python
    def __post_init__(self):
        valid_types = {"text", "textarea", "select", "date", "number", "checkbox"}
        if self.field_type not in valid_types:
            raise ValueError(
                f"FieldDef '{self.name}': invalid field_type '{self.field_type}'. "
                f"Must be one of: {', '.join(sorted(valid_types))}"
            )
        if self.field_type == "select" and self.source is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"FieldDef '{self.name}': field_type 'select' requires a 'source'."
            )
```

### AFTER

```python
    def __post_init__(self):
        valid_types = {
            "text", "textarea", "select", "date", "number", "checkbox", "hidden",
        }
        if self.field_type not in valid_types:
            raise ValueError(
                f"FieldDef '{self.name}': invalid field_type '{self.field_type}'. "
                f"Must be one of: {', '.join(sorted(valid_types))}"
            )
        if self.field_type == "select" and self.source is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"FieldDef '{self.name}': field_type 'select' requires a 'source'."
            )
```

### Why

- `hidden` needs to be a legal `field_type` for fieldkit's `_build_field()`
  to produce a `FieldDef` for `project_id`/`parent_id` on tasks without
  raising at startup.
- No other validation changes: a hidden field has no special
  requirement analogous to `select`'s `source` — `required`, `readonly`,
  `source`, `placeholder`, and `help_text` remain meaningful (or
  harmlessly unused) exactly as they are for every other type.
- Also update the module docstring's `FieldDef.field_type` doc comment
  (`"One of: text, textarea, select, date, number, checkbox."`) to
  include `hidden` in that list, since it's the field-level
  documentation of the same valid-types set:

```python
        field_type: Input type. One of: text, textarea, select, date,
                    number, checkbox, hidden. Defaults to 'text'.
```

---

## Apply and deploy — full sequence

Confirmed 2026-07-10: `viewkit` is installed as a **regular
(non-editable)** package in Curator's venv (copied into
`site-packages`, not linked to the `dev-utils` repo). Editing the repo
source alone does nothing until reinstalled.

1. Edit `~/projects/dev-utils/python/viewkit/models.py` per the diff above.
2. Commit and push to GitHub per normal `dev-utils` workflow.
3. Reinstall into Curator's venv (from `~/projects/curator`, `.venv` active):

   ```bash
   pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps /home/carolyn/projects/dev-utils/python/viewkit
   ```

   `--no-deps` avoids pip also touching `dbkit`/`pyyaml` unnecessarily.
   `--force-reinstall` is required because the version number
   (`0.1.0`) isn't changing — without it, pip sees the same version
   already installed and skips the reinstall silently.

4. Restart uvicorn to pick up the new code (already-imported modules in
   a running process won't see the change either way, editable install
   or not).

## Not in scope here

- Making `viewkit` an editable install (`pip install -e
  ~/projects/dev-utils/python/viewkit`) so future `viewkit` changes
  don't need step 3's reinstall dance. Worth doing at some point since

  convenience change, not required to unblock this work — noted here,
  not actioned.
- Any bump to `viewkit`'s version number (`0.1.0`). Left unchanged;
  revisit if/when `viewkit` gets a real versioning discipline.
- The Curator-side consumers of this new `hidden` type
  (`fieldkit_overrides.yaml`, `_detail_form_fields.html`, `panel.py`,
  `tasks.py`) — separate changedoc, Curator repo, depends on this one
  being applied and reinstalled first.
